transcript: On the surface, it might seem obvious why Oh Mary is such a big success on Broadway, right? People love it, it's inexpensive to run each week, and the replacement casting has been brilliant. But there's something in that last point that I don't think we talk about enough. Celebrity casting on Broadway is famously everywhere, but it feels like the narrative around that casting is usually more like the producers trying to court celebrities, trying to convince celebrities to come to Broadway. Or alternatively, if it's the celebrity's idea, then the project is usually built around them. But all that to say, it seems like getting celebrities to come in as a replacement has been historically very difficult to do *sustainably* as in over the course of an extended run. But that does not seem to be the case with Oh Mary at all. Cole Escola made this joke on the red carpet about, like, everyone wait your turn, you'll all get a chance to play Mary. But it does seem like there's some truth to that. Like celebrities are lining up to play this role in a way that I don't think I've ever seen in another Broadway production to this extent. And I think that's the case not just because people love this show, but also because Escola has written a role that is the perfect mix of flashy and technically doable. You know, comedy is never easy. Broadway is never easy. But it does seem like the femands of the role are such that people who are not necessarily as experienced Broadway performers can play it. So they are both casting a wide net and using irresistible bait. And I really think that intersection, more so than the buzz, more so even than the low running cost, has been the secret ingredient for their financial success on Broadway.
classificationReason: Discussion and analysis of Oh Mary's replacement casting phenomenon and celebrity appeal. No first-hand review of seeing the show; purely commentary about the production's casting dynamics.
